performers: Mary Garden, soprano; Claude Debussy, piano
intro: Mary Garden sings Verlaine’s rain-soaked sorrow with Debussy himself at the piano, in Paris in 1904. His running semiquavers keep falling beneath a voice that cannot explain its grief.

sections.label: A · Rain in the piano
sections.mNote: Long vocal notes stretch above running semiquavers

sections.label: B · The rain pauses for a question
sections.mNote: The piano breaks into chords beneath freer singing

sections.label: A′ · Rain beneath the last stanza
sections.mNote: The semiquavers return and outlast the voice

cues.title: Rain in the piano
cues.text: The piano sets fine semiquavers pattering beneath the song. Against their quick movement, the singer’s notes stretch out, marked triste et monotone — sad and monotonous. Verlaine’s falling rain and inward tears have different speeds.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Ariettes oubliées, no. 2, voice-and-piano score, printed pp. 12–13: pp, con sordine, running semiquavers and the vocal marking triste et monotone. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/8/83/IMSLP14819-Debussy_-_Ariettes_oubli%C3%A9es_%28voice_and_piano%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sorrow without a cause
cues.text: Verlaine’s rain falls on roofs and the ground. Inside, someone grieves without knowing why: no betrayal, no love or hatred to account for the pain. The poem appears in Romances sans paroles in 1874. Debussy gives its unsettled heart a line that keeps circling back.
cues.evidence: Paul Verlaine, Il pleure dans mon cœur, Romances sans paroles (1874), all four stanzas. French text: https://press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/853446.html. Recurrent vocal phrases are visible in the song score, pp. 12–17.

cues.title: The rain returns
cues.text: After the freer question about betrayal, the piano’s running notes come back. The final stanza names the worst pain: not knowing why the heart aches. The voice slows and finishes; the piano carries the rain on alone.
cues.evidence: Voice-and-piano score, pp. 15–17: Modéré question, Revenez au 1er Mouvement, final stanza at 1° Tempo, Molto rallentando and piano postlude.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The semiquavers stop for the voice
transitions.to: B · The rain pauses for a question
transitions.how: The piano’s running semiquavers stop. Debussy cancels the four-sharp key signature and marks the passage Modéré, allowing the voice to move freely over chords and a short piano reply. The poem asks whether betrayal explains the grief; the regular patter of rain is suspended.
transitions.evidence: Voice-and-piano score, printed pp. 15–16: cancelled key signature, Modéré, ad libitum and the question beginning Quoi! nulle trahison?

transitions.title: Semiquavers carry the last stanza
transitions.from: B · The rain pauses for a question
transitions.to: A′ · Rain beneath the last stanza
transitions.how: The piano resumes its semiquavers while the voice holds the end of the word raison. Revenez au 1er Mouvement brings back the opening pace; the four-sharp signature returns with the final stanza. The singer’s long notes again stretch above the quick piano figure.
transitions.evidence: Voice-and-piano score, printed p. 16: semiquavers beneath the held vocal note, Revenez au 1er Mouvement and restored four-sharp signature at 1° Tempo.

source.title: Debussy, Ariettes oubliées no.2 · voice-and-piano score
source.locator: No. 2, printed pp. 12–17: running piano semiquavers, the freer central question and the piano postlude.

timeline.note: Semiquavers patter quietly in the piano.
Long vocal notes stretch above the piano’s running semiquavers.
The voice asks about betrayal; the piano’s semiquavers stop.
Running semiquavers return beneath the final stanza.
The piano keeps the rain falling after the voice falls silent.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
